before.content_html:
War as a Factor in Medical Progress

An estimated 18–20 million died in World War One and 50–80 million in World War Two. This mass suffering created an urgent need for medical innovation, driving rapid advances in surgery, treatment, and technology. War has appeared again and again as a driving force behind medical change. The pressure of saving lives in extreme conditions speeds up innovation that might otherwise take decades. This lesson traces that thread from the medieval battlefield to the modern operating theatre.

Key Fact

War accelerates medical progress for three main reasons: it creates urgency (thousands of wounded need treating), it provides funding (governments invest heavily in wartime medicine), and it offers a testing ground (new techniques can be tried on a massive scale).

Medieval & Renaissance Warfare: Ambroise Paré

In the sixteenth century, the standard treatment for gunshot wounds was to pour boiling oil into the wound to “cauterise” it. The French barber-surgeon Ambroise Paré changed this by accident. During the siege of Turin in 1537, he ran out of boiling oil and improvised a mixture of egg yolk, rose oil, and turpentine. Soldiers treated with the salve healed better and suffered less pain.

Key Fact

Paré also promoted the use of ligatures — threads of silk tied around blood vessels during amputation to control bleeding, replacing the agonising method of cauterisation with a hot iron. However, ligatures carried a risk of infection, a problem that would not be solved until the development of antiseptic surgery centuries later.

The Crimean War & Nursing: Florence Nightingale

The Crimean War (1853–1856) exposed the terrible state of military hospitals. At the British base hospital in Scutari, soldiers were dying not from their wounds but from infections, cholera, and dysentery caused by filthy conditions. Florence Nightingale arrived in 1854 with 38 nurses and transformed the hospital.

Key Fact

Nightingale’s reforms at Scutari cut the death rate from 42% to just 2%. She insisted on scrubbing the wards, providing clean bedding, improving ventilation, and serving nutritious food. She used statistical evidence — including her famous “coxcomb” diagrams — to prove that most deaths were caused by preventable diseases, not battle injuries.

After the war, Nightingale campaigned for reform. She published Notes on Nursing (1859) and set up the Nightingale Training School at St Thomas’ Hospital in 1860, making nursing a profession for the first time. She also shaped hospital design, insisting on well-ventilated “pavilion” wards with good sanitation.

Nightingale proved that clean, well-organised hospitals saved lives — a principle behind all of modern healthcare. She also showed the power of using data to drive medical reform.

World War I & II: A Surgical Revolution

The two World Wars produced medical advances on a huge scale. Millions of wounded soldiers and massive government funding created the conditions for major breakthroughs.

X-Rays on the Battlefield

X-rays, discovered by Wilhelm Röntgen in 1895, became essential in WWI for locating bullets, shrapnel, and fractures. Marie Curie developed mobile X-ray units — “petites Curies” — mounted in vehicles driven to field hospitals near the front lines. By the end of WWI, over a million soldiers had been X-rayed.

Blood Transfusions

Before WWI, blood transfusions were unreliable and dangerous. Karl Landsteiner had identified blood groups (A, B, AB, O) in 1901, but mass wartime casualties drove their practical use. During WWI, doctors learned to store blood using sodium citrate (which stopped it clotting). By WWII, the first blood banks were set up, giving a reliable supply for treating battlefield casualties.

Plastic Surgery

The horrific facial injuries caused by trench warfare in WWI led to modern plastic surgery. Harold Gillies, from New Zealand, set up a dedicated ward at the Queen’s Hospital in Sidcup, Kent, developing techniques to rebuild faces destroyed by shrapnel and burns. His cousin, Archibald McIndoe, advanced these techniques during WWII, treating RAF pilots with severe burns.

Just as Paré had to innovate when facing new types of gunshot wounds in the 1500s, Gillies faced new injuries caused by high-explosive shells. In both cases, new weapons demanded new surgical responses — and the pressure of treating devastating injuries on a massive scale drove surgeons to develop techniques that would have been unthinkable in peacetime.

Penicillin: From Laboratory to Mass Production

Penicillin was discovered by Alexander Fleming in 1928, but WWII turned it from a lab curiosity into a life-saving drug. Howard Florey and Ernst Chain developed methods to produce it in usable amounts, and the US government funded mass production to treat wounded soldiers. By D-Day (June 1944), there was enough penicillin to treat every Allied casualty.

Key Fact

Penicillin is one of the clearest examples of how war accelerates medical progress. Fleming discovered it in 1928, but without the urgency of WWII and the funding from the US government, mass production might have taken many more years. By 1944, penicillin was saving thousands of lives on the battlefield — and after the war, it revolutionised civilian medicine too.

The Carrel-Dakin Method

Before antibiotics, one of the most important WWI wound-care advances was the Carrel-Dakin method. Surgeon Alexis Carrel and chemist Henry Dakin developed a technique of continuously running an antiseptic solution — sodium hypochlorite — through wounds using tubes. It killed bacteria and cut infection rates sharply. The method was a vital bridge between Lister’s antiseptic techniques and the antibiotic revolution that came with penicillin.

War & Public Health

War also transformed public health policy by exposing the poor health of the general population.

During the Boer War (1899–1902), up to 40% of army volunteers were rejected as medically unfit. They were too short, underweight, or ill from diseases caused by poverty. If Britain could not raise a healthy army, how could it defend its empire?

The result was the Liberal Reforms (1906–1914): free school meals, school medical inspections, old age pensions, and the National Insurance Act of 1911. For the first time, the government took responsibility for its citizens’ health.

Both World Wars deepened public expectations that the government should provide healthcare. WWI soldiers returned expecting a “land fit for heroes” — though many felt betrayed by the lack of reform that followed.

In WWII, shared sacrifice on the Home Front — rationing, the Blitz, evacuation — fuelled demand for a fairer society. The Beveridge Report (1942) and the Emergency Medical Service proved a state-run health system could work. The result was the NHS in 1948.

Timeline: Key War-Related Medical Breakthroughs

1537

Paré’s discovery at the Siege of Turin

Runs out of boiling oil and discovers that a soothing salve of egg yolk, rose oil, and turpentine heals gunshot wounds better. Also promotes silk ligatures.

1854

Nightingale transforms Scutari Hospital

Cuts the death rate from 42% to 2% through strict hygiene, clean bedding, ventilation, and nutritious food during the Crimean War.

1899–1902

Boer War exposes the nation’s poor health

Up to 40% of army volunteers rejected as medically unfit. Leads to the Liberal Reforms of 1906–1914.

1914–1918

World War I surgical advances

Mobile X-ray units (Marie Curie), blood transfusions using stored blood, and Harold Gillies’ pioneering plastic surgery for facial injuries.

1939–1945

World War II — penicillin and the road to the NHS

Mass production of penicillin, blood banks established, Emergency Medical Service proves state-run healthcare works. Beveridge Report published 1942.

1948

The NHS is created

Born from wartime solidarity and the Beveridge Report. Free, universal healthcare for the first time in British history.

Modern Technology and Surgery

War drove surgical progress for centuries, but in the late twentieth and early twenty-first centuries, technology has become an equally powerful force for change. Many wartime breakthroughs have been refined and expanded by peacetime research.

Transplant Surgery

In 1967, South African surgeon Christiaan Barnard performed the world’s first successful human heart transplant. The patient, Louis Washkansky, survived for 18 days. Early patients often died from organ rejection, but immunosuppressant drugs (especially cyclosporine in the 1980s) greatly improved survival rates.

Keyhole & Robotic Surgery

Keyhole (laparoscopic) surgery changed operations from the 1980s onwards. Instead of large incisions, surgeons insert tiny cameras and instruments through small cuts. This means less pain, smaller scars, shorter hospital stays, and faster recovery.

Robotic surgery takes this further. Systems like the da Vinci surgical robot (introduced in 2000) allow surgeons to control robotic arms with greater precision than the human hand, making extremely delicate operations possible.

Scanning Technology

Modern technology has transformed doctors’ ability to see inside the body without surgery. CT scans (1970s) use X-rays from multiple angles to build detailed cross-sectional images. MRI scans (1980s) use magnetic fields to produce even more detailed images of soft tissues, including the brain. Both allow doctors to diagnose conditions without exploratory surgery.

Key Fact

The journey from Röntgen’s X-ray (1895) to Marie Curie’s mobile units on the WWI battlefield to modern CT and MRI scanners shows how wartime innovation laid the foundations for peacetime technology. Each advance built on the last, transforming what doctors could see, diagnose, and treat.

before.content_html:
The Paradox of Progress

Modern public health is, in many ways, a victim of its own success. Vaccination, antibiotics, better sanitation, and the NHS have all extended life expectancy. But living longer has created new challenges. The diseases that dominate modern Britain are not the infectious epidemics of the past, but long-term degenerative conditions and illnesses linked to the way we live.

Key Fact

In 1900, average life expectancy in Britain was around 47 years. By 2020, it had risen to over 81 years. This extraordinary improvement is the result of centuries of medical progress — but it means today’s biggest health challenges are diseases of old age and lifestyle, not the infectious diseases that once killed millions.

New Diseases & Lifestyle Challenges

Long-Term Degenerative Conditions

As people live longer, the biggest medical challenges are conditions where the body slowly breaks down over time. These include:

  • Cancer — abnormal cell growth that can affect almost any part of the body. Risk increases significantly with age.
  • Alzheimer’s disease — a progressive brain disorder that destroys memory and cognitive function. It is the most common cause of dementia.
  • Parkinson’s disease — a condition affecting movement, causing tremors, stiffness, and difficulty with balance and coordination.

Lifestyle Diseases

Many of today’s most common illnesses are linked to modern lifestyles — poor diet, lack of exercise, smoking, and heavy drinking. These lifestyle diseases include:

  • Type 2 diabetes — strongly linked to obesity and poor diet. Cases have risen dramatically in recent decades.
  • Heart disease — the leading cause of death in the UK, linked to smoking, high-fat diets, and lack of exercise.
  • Some cancers — including lung cancer (linked to smoking), liver cancer (linked to alcohol), and bowel cancer (linked to processed meat and low-fibre diets).

Mental Health

Mental health is now one of the biggest public health challenges. Depression, anxiety, and eating disorders affect millions in Britain. Mental health services have always received less funding than physical health, despite affecting a similar number of people. Stigma has also made it harder for people to seek help, though awareness campaigns have begun to change this.

Antibiotic Resistance

One of the most serious global health threats today is antibiotic resistance. Decades of overusing antibiotics — in both human medicine and farming — have created superbugs: bacteria that have evolved to survive the drugs designed to kill them.

Key Fact

MRSA is one of the best-known superbugs. If antibiotic resistance continues to grow, routine operations like hip replacements, caesarean sections, and even dental surgery could become life-threatening because doctors would be unable to prevent or treat post-operative infections. The World Health Organization has called antibiotic resistance “one of the biggest threats to global health.”

Antibiotics have been overprescribed for decades — given for viral infections (where they have no effect), not finished by patients (letting partly resistant bacteria survive), and used routinely in farming to promote growth. Each time antibiotics are used wrongly, it gives bacteria a chance to evolve resistance.

At the same time, drug companies have invested less in new antibiotics because they are less profitable than drugs for long-term conditions. The result is a growing gap between resistant infections and the drugs available to treat them.

Challenges for the NHS

An Ageing Population

Britain’s population is ageing. Better healthcare and rising life expectancy mean more people are living into their 80s and 90s. This is a triumph of medical progress, but it puts huge pressure on the NHS. Older people are far more likely to have chronic conditions — heart disease, diabetes, dementia — that need expensive, ongoing care.

Key Fact

People aged 65 and over account for around 40% of NHS spending, despite making up less than 20% of the population. As the proportion of elderly people grows, the financial pressure on the NHS will only increase — raising difficult questions about how healthcare is funded and prioritised.

Rising Costs & Expectations

Modern medicine can achieve extraordinary things — but at huge cost. Treatments like chemotherapy, radiotherapy, robotic surgery, and gene therapy are all expensive. The NHS now costs around £201 billion per year to run. At the same time, public expectations have risen — people expect the latest treatments and shorter waiting times. Balancing demand against limited resources is one of the NHS’s greatest ongoing challenges.

Government Public Health Campaigns

Faced with rising lifestyle diseases, governments have used campaigns and laws to change behaviour and prevent illness. This continues the tradition of government action in public health that stretches back to the Public Health Acts of the nineteenth century.

Smoking bans: England banned smoking in enclosed public places in 2007. Smoking rates have fallen sharply, reducing lung cancer, heart disease, and respiratory illness.

Sugar tax: The 2018 Soft Drinks Industry Levy pushes manufacturers to cut sugar in drinks. It targets childhood obesity and type 2 diabetes.

Alcohol limits: Government campaigns promote lower recommended limits (14 units per week) to reduce liver disease, some cancers, and alcohol-related harm.

COVID-19 response: The COVID-19 pandemic (2020–2021) was the most dramatic government public health action in living memory. National lockdowns, mass testing, and the fastest vaccine rollout in history showed the scale of modern intervention — but also exposed inequalities in health outcomes based on income, ethnicity, and geography.

The Rise of Alternative Medicine & Skepticism

Despite huge advances in modern medicine, interest has grown in alternative medicine — treatments like acupuncture, aromatherapy, homeopathy, and hypnotherapy that sit outside mainstream evidence-based medicine. Some people turn to these when conventional medicine cannot cure their condition, or because they prefer a more “natural” approach.

Vaccine Skepticism

A more dangerous trend is growing vaccine skepticism. In 1998, Andrew Wakefield published a fraudulent study claiming the MMR vaccine caused autism. The study was later thoroughly discredited — Wakefield was struck off the medical register and the paper was retracted — but the damage was done. Vaccination rates dropped, and measles — almost eliminated — began to return.

Key Fact

The MMR scare is a powerful example of how misinformation can undermine public health. Lower vaccination rates in some areas led to outbreaks of measles — a preventable disease. It demonstrates that public health progress is never permanent and can be reversed by loss of public trust.

The Thalidomide Disaster

Key Fact

The thalidomide disaster is one of modern medicine’s most important warnings. In the late 1950s, thalidomide was prescribed to pregnant women for morning sickness. It caused severe birth defects — thousands of babies were born with shortened or missing limbs. The scandal led to much stricter drug testing and regulation, and is a stark reminder that thorough testing is essential before treatments reach patients.

Genetic Medicine & DNA

One of the most exciting areas of modern medicine is genetic medicine — using knowledge of DNA and genes to prevent, diagnose, and treat disease. This field has been transformed by the Human Genome Project.

1953

Watson and Crick discover the structure of DNA

James Watson and Francis Crick (building on Rosalind Franklin’s X-ray work) identify the double-helix structure of DNA, the molecule that carries genetic instructions for all living things.

1990–2003

The Human Genome Project

An international project to map the entire human genetic code. It identified approximately 20,000–25,000 human genes and created the foundation for genetic medicine.

2000s onwards

Gene therapy trials begin

Gene therapy — replacing or repairing faulty genes to treat disease — enters clinical trials for conditions including certain cancers, inherited blindness, and blood disorders.

Present day

Personalised medicine

Personalised medicine allows treatments to be tailored to a patient’s individual genetic profile. Cancer patients, for example, can have their tumour’s DNA analysed to find the most effective drug for their specific type.

Key Fact — Genetic Testing in Practice

In 2013, actress Angelina Jolie publicly announced that genetic testing had revealed she carried a mutated BRCA1 gene, giving her a very high risk of developing breast cancer — her mother, grandmother, and aunt had all died of cancer. She chose to have a preventative double mastectomy to reduce her risk. This high-profile case showed how DNA knowledge can now allow people to take preventative action against diseases they have not yet developed — a revolutionary shift from treating illness after it appears to preventing it before it begins.

Genetic medicine fits into the broader course narrative. Just as Jenner’s vaccination, Pasteur’s germ theory, and Fleming’s penicillin each changed everything, genetic medicine could transform twenty-first century healthcare. It also raises ethical questions about privacy, cost, and access — echoing debates about the NHS and public health throughout the course.

Show awareness of modern developments and connect them to broader themes — especially the role of science and technology in medical change.
